result.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
result.summary: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

AI.brief_summary: 论文提出「Resolution Hypothesis」，认为 agent 自我进化停滞并非因为提不出更好的 artifact（prompt、skill、memory），而是因为带噪评估无法可靠识别改进；作者在候选选择与方法排名两个层面，用七种进化方法与六个模型（超千万次 LLM 调用）检验该假设。
AI.relevance_reason: 其候选级选择接近随机、方法级差距小于同方法重跑波动的诊断，可供核查 LVR 训练轨迹筛选与 latent 策略比较中「真实增益是否可分辨」，提示小幅度性能提升可能只是评估噪声而非机制有效。
